jsnvu6-e184009-d1e106.summary: Rubric for Question 3 of d.25: whether infused faith suffices to elicit the act of faith without acquired faith, referring to Cajetan and Aquinas.

jsnvu6-e184009-d1e117.summary: Argument that infused faith suffices: a habit is that which one can use at will when the object is present, which would not be true unless infused faith could issue in act without any acquired faith.
claims: A habit by definition suffices for its act when the object is present (objection)

jsnvu6-e184009-d1e133.summary: Second argument: infused faith is more perfect than acquired faith, and acquired faith can act without infused; so infused faith can act without acquired.
claims: The more perfect infused faith should act without acquired faith (objection)

jsnvu6-e184009-d1e145.summary: Argument for the opposite: 'how shall they believe him of whom they have not heard?' and 'faith comes by hearing' (Rom. 10); faith from hearing is acquired, so acquired faith is needed for belief.
claims: Belief requires faith from hearing, which is acquired

jsnvu6-e184009-d1e158.summary: Determination: infused faith does not suffice without acquired faith, understood as any cognition received from apparent things. First proof: otherwise a baptized person with infused faith, grown up and miraculously endowed with natural science, would assent to the articles and reject their opposites without any persuasion, which is false. Jews already believing some things did not assent to Christ's new articles by faith alone; those who did were aided by knowledge acquired from his life and miracles. A person with only natural knowledge would more readily believe one divine supposit than three and that God is not man. And Augustine says he would not believe the Gospel unless the Church approved it, an assent that is acquired.
claims: Infused faith does not suffice for the act of belief without acquired cognition from apparent things
Assent to new articles requires acquired knowledge such as from miracles
Natural reason alone would incline against the Trinity and Incarnation
Assent dependent on the Church's approval is acquired

jsnvu6-e184009-d1e249.summary: Second proof: an act about a non-apparent object that depends on something apparent cannot come from an infused habit alone, which does not make its object apparent; belief in the articles must resolve to a middle apparent in itself, as shown earlier. Christ confirms this (John 15: had I not spoken and done works, they would have no sin), which would be false if infused faith sufficed once credibles were proposed. So Paul says preaching is needed (Rom. 10), and preaching is not bare proposal but persuasion from Scripture, signs, or something apparent.
claims: Belief must resolve to something apparent, which infused faith does not supply
Unbelief without preaching and miracles would be excusable
Preaching involves persuasion from Scripture or signs, not mere proposal

jsnvu6-e184009-d1e299.summary: Reply to the first argument: the definition of habit as what one uses at will applies to acquired habits generated by acts and producing readiness and facility, not to infused habits.
claims: The definition 'habit is what one uses at will' applies to acquired, not infused, habits

jsnvu6-e184009-d1e312.summary: Reply to the second: grace presupposes nature and not conversely; so cognition by naturally acquired habit can exist without infused habit, but cognition through infused grace cannot exist without some naturally acquired knowledge.
claims: Infused cognition requires some naturally acquired knowledge

jsnvu6-e184009.summary: Question 3 of d.25 asks whether infused faith suffices to elicit the act of belief without acquired faith, meaning any cognition received from apparent things. Durandus denies that it does. A baptized person with infused faith but no persuasion would not assent to the articles over their opposites, and natural reason would rather incline against the Trinity and Incarnation. Jews who already believed did not accept Christ's new articles by faith alone; those who did were aided by his life and miracles. Augustine believed the Gospel because of the Church's approval, which is acquired assent. Belief about non-apparent objects must resolve to something apparent, which an infused habit cannot supply. Christ says unbelief would be excusable without his words and works, and Paul makes preaching, understood as persuasion from Scripture or signs, necessary. The definition of habit as 'usable at will' applies to acquired habits, and since grace presupposes nature, infused cognition requires some naturally acquired knowledge.
claims: Infused faith does not suffice for the act of belief without acquired cognition
Belief must resolve to something apparent, such as miracles or the Church's approval
Preaching with persuasion is necessary for belief
Grace presupposes nature, so infused cognition presupposes acquired knowledge
